pages.text: The Panchatantra is one of the oldest collections of stories in the world. It was written in Sanskrit in ancient India, probably around 300 BCE, though some scholars believe the stories are older still. The word Panchatantra means five chapters or five strategies. The stories were designed to teach young princes how to govern wisely, to understand human nature, and to navigate the world with intelligence.

image.note: Illustration: an elderly scholar reading from a palm-leaf manuscript to a group of young princes

pages.text: Like Aesop's fables, the Panchatantra uses animals as characters. But where Aesop's stories tend to be short and direct, Panchatantra stories are often nested: a story contains another story within it, which may contain yet another. A character telling a tale to make a point tells a tale in which a character tells another tale. The stories wrap around each other like the coils of a snake.

The Panchatantra has influenced storytelling traditions all over the world. Its stories spread from India to Persia, from Persia to Arabia, from Arabia to Europe. Many of the stories that appear in One Thousand and One Nights, and many European fairy tales, trace their origin to the Panchatantra. It is one of the most widely translated books in human history.
This is the story that first appeared at Level 4. Now it is told in full.

image.note: Illustration: a monkey sitting in a fruit tree on a riverbank, a crocodile visible in the water below

pages.text: A monkey lived in a tree on the bank of a river, full of fruit. A crocodile visited each day, and the monkey threw fruit down to him. They became friends. The crocodile's wife grew jealous. 'If the fruit he eats is so sweet,' she said, 'imagine how sweet his heart must be. Bring me his heart.' The crocodile was sorrowful, but he agreed. He invited the monkey to visit his home under the river.

'I cannot swim,' said the monkey. 'I will carry you,' said the crocodile. 'Ride on my back.' The monkey climbed on. When they were in the middle of the river, the crocodile told his friend the truth. 'I need your heart,' he said. 'My wife demands it.' The monkey was afraid, but he thought quickly. 'But I left my heart in the tree,' he said. 'I never carry it with me when I travel. Take me back and I will get it.' The crocodile turned and swam back. The monkey leaped to the tree. 'Go,' he said. 'A friend who would kill me at another's demand is no friend at all.'
Moral: Test your friends before you trust them. And never let another person's jealousy destroy what is good.

A pair of crows built a nest in a great tree. But in the hollow of the same tree lived a large serpent, who ate their eggs each year. The male crow despaired. The female crow went to seek advice from a clever jackal.

image.note: Illustration: two crows in a tree nest, a snake coiled in a hollow below

pages.text: 'Go to the royal lake early in the morning,' said the jackal. 'The princess will be bathing, with her attendants on the bank. Steal the most valuable piece of jewellery you can find and carry it back, making sure the guards see you. Drop it into the serpent's hollow.' The crow did as the jackal instructed. The guards followed, found the serpent, and killed it to retrieve the jewellery. The crows were safe.
Moral: When strength is not enough, use intelligence. A clever plan can solve what force cannot.

Here is another tale the old teacher told. A flock of pigeons, hunting for food, spotted grain scattered beneath a tree and swooped down together, only to find themselves trapped under a hunter's net. As the hunter approached, the wise leader of the flock had an idea. On my command, he said, every one of you beat your wings at once, and we will carry the net away together. Alone, each pigeon was helpless. Together, they lifted the net into the sky.

They flew, net and all, to the home of a mouse who was the leader's friend, and the mouse gnawed through the cords and set them free. A crow, watching all this, was so impressed by the friendship between pigeon and mouse that he begged the mouse to be his friend too. And so a new tale began, for in the Panchatantra one friendship always leads to another, and every creature's cleverness is worth more when it is shared.

chapters.title: The Four Friends and the Hunter

pages.text: A deer, a tortoise, a crow, and a mouse were friends. They lived near a lake in the forest. One day, the deer was caught in a hunter's trap.

image.note: Illustration: a deer tangled in a net, a crow watching from above, a tortoise and mouse on the ground below

pages.text: The crow flew ahead to warn the hunter's approach. The mouse gnawed through the net to free the deer. But now the tortoise, who had come to watch, was in the hunter's path. 'I will carry you,' said the deer. The crow flew ahead to distract the hunter. The mouse and the tortoise hid. The deer carried the tortoise to safety.
The hunter reached the empty net and found nothing. 'I was undone,' he said, 'by creatures with no weapons at all.' He was right. They had no weapons. They had something better: each other.
Moral: Friendship between those with different strengths is the most powerful force of all.

A king was proud of his own wisdom. He dismissed his most experienced minister, an old man who had served three kings before him. 'I have no need of old advisers,' he said. 'I am clever enough to govern alone.' Within six months, the king had made three costly mistakes in foreign policy, alienated two neighbouring kingdoms, and lost a significant trade route.

image.note: Illustration: a young king on a throne looking troubled; an old minister waiting patiently outside the palace door

pages.text: He summoned the old minister back. 'I was wrong,' he said. 'Not about your wisdom,' said the minister, 'but about what wisdom is. Wisdom is not cleverness. Cleverness gets you to the right answer quickly. Wisdom tells you which questions to ask first. You had cleverness. You still need wisdom. That is why I am here.' The king listened more carefully after that.
Moral: Cleverness and wisdom are not the same thing. Both matter. Wisdom knows which one to use first.

The old teacher had one final lesson for the young princes. A brahmin was given a goat to carry home for a sacrifice. Three thieves, wanting the goat, hatched a plan. One by one, at three points along the road, each thief stopped the brahmin and asked why a holy man was carrying a dog on his shoulders. By the third time, the brahmin was so unsettled that he became convinced the goat truly was a dog, dropped it, and hurried home. The thieves collected their prize.

A lie told once may be laughed off, said the teacher, but a lie repeated by many voices can overturn what a man sees with his own eyes. Guard your judgement. That is why these stories matter to a future ruler: a king is surrounded by voices, each with its own purpose, and the one who cannot tell flattery from counsel, or a rumour from a fact, will lose his goat, and in time his kingdom. Wisdom is knowing which voices to believe.
